title: The Waters Recede, God Promises
overview: The floodwaters slowly go down, Noah and the animals leave the ark, and God promises never again to destroy all life this way.

parts.label: The waters go down (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: In Hebrew, God remembering someone means he turns to act for them, not that he had forgotten them, and here he sends a wind and stops the rain and the waters from below. The waters drain slowly over months until the ark settles in the mountains of Ararat, a region around today's eastern Turkey and Armenia, though the exact peak is unknown.

parts.label: The raven and the dove (vv. 6-12)
parts.note: Noah sends out birds to test whether the land is dry: the raven keeps flying back and forth, and the dove returns until it brings a fresh olive leaf, proof that trees are growing again. When the dove finally does not come back, it has found a place to live, and Noah's patient seven day waits show him reading the signs rather than being told.

parts.label: Coming out of the ark (vv. 13-19)
parts.note: By the story's own dates, Noah has been in the ark about a year, and even after the ground is dry he waits for God to tell him to leave. God sends the animals out to multiply and fill the earth, echoing the blessing given to living things at creation.

parts.label: Noah's offering (vv. 20-21a)
parts.note: Noah's first act is a burnt offering, an animal burned whole on an altar as a gift to God, using "clean" animals, the kinds considered fit for this. Saying God smelled its pleasing scent is human language for God accepting the gift.

parts.label: God's change of course (v. 21b)
parts.note: God says people's hearts lean toward evil from youth, the same problem behind the flood in chapter 6, yet he vows never again to curse the ground or destroy all living things. Many readers take this to mean the promise rests on God's patience rather than on people improving, though that is an interpretation.

parts.label: Seasons will not stop (v. 22)
parts.note: The promise itself is that planting and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, and day and night will keep going as long as the earth lasts. For people who lived by farming, this was a pledge that the world would stay steady enough to live in.

think: This promise is made while openly admitting that people have not changed. Is it possible to stay committed to someone without expecting them to become better, and what would that cost?
